newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Lower S.Korea interest rates no help to small firm.
newsitem.headline: Lower S.Korea interest rates no help to small firm.

text.p: South Korean interest rates have dropped to their lowest levels in nearly a year but analysts said on Tuesday the decline had provided little relief so far for the many smaller companies suffering from cash shortages.
A series of corporate failures, beginning with the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co in January, had left lenders jittery, distorting the country's money market, analysts said.

The one-day call market rate, an indicator of short-term market liquidity, currently stands at about 10 percent, compared with an average of 11.5 percent in June 1996. Benchmark three-year corporate bonds closed at a new 1997 low for the fourth consecutive session on Monday, the lowest close in nearly 12 months.
However, yields rebounded to 11.42 percent on Tuesday on central bank intervention. Dealers said the central bank seemed to believe the recent downturn in rates had been too "steep and fast".
"Liquid financial institutions have switched their interest to more stable equity-linked investments such as bonds and stocks," said Kang Yung-gee, a bond trader at Hyundai Securities.
The Seoul stock market recorded a new yearly high of 775.01 on Monday, underpinned by high cash liquidity and hopes for an economic turnaround based on the Japanese yen's renewed vigour.
"The money market is fairly distorted. The rich get richer and the poor get poorer," said Kim Hyeok-eon, a bond dealer at Daishin Securities.
Bankers said domestic financial institutions, which months ago could pick and choose among loan candidates, remained fluid and were now scrambling to lend, especially to top tier groups.
But the most attractive companies have favoured direct financing methods.

Meanwhile, smaller companies have struggled to borrow as lenders increasingly refuse fresh loans unless borrowers can prove their financial structure is healthy or unless they produce substantial collateral.

"There are many foreign banks that would like to deal with only the top five conglomerates. Most bankers have become very selective and conservative in their loan operations," said Ahn Jae-wook, operations manager at Seoul branch of National Australia Bank.
Lee Sang-tae, an economist at Korea Federation of Small Business, said 1,318 smaller companies defaulted on their debts in April, compared to 936 a year ago.
Discount rates offered from the black money market on smaller firms' promissory notes have risen to 31 percent from the previous 23.7 percent.
"But small companies cannot find enough lenders despite the high rates. It's really serious," Lee said.

Analysts blamed a slew of defaults by affiliate companies of financially troubled conglomerates. Hanbo's failure was followed by Sammi Steel Co in March. A number of high-profile business groups have announced restructuring plans to avert failure.

Alarmed by widespread rumours of financial crisis, Finance and Economy Minsiter Kang Kyong-shik last month warned financial companies of moving too quickly to call in debts of firms rumoured to be in trouble. He said lenders' eagerness to act on rumours had caused severe cash-flow problems among local firms.
Dealers partly attributed falling rates to slow money demand as domestic companies, hit by an economic slowdown, have reduced their investments.
"The interest rates are heading for an era of single digits," Kang of Hyundai said.
